children: 0553 GMT - The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield shows a rising risk of a deeper pullback on the weekly chart, says Quek Ser Leang of UOB Global Economics & Markets Research in a note. Last week's pullback has continued and is gathering momentum this week, the senior technical strategist notes. Although this week has yet to conclude, the 10-year yield is on course for its largest weekly drop since late July. Also, the weekly relative strength index is unwinding swiftly from overbought levels. A break below 5.021% could lead to a fall toward the 21-week exponential moving average, which is now near 4.81%, the strategist adds. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield is little changed at 5.0863%, FactSet data show. (ronnie.harui@wsj.com)

0543 GMT - U.S. Treasury yields may have reached levels where their elevated levels weigh on risk sentiment, SEB's Jussi Hiljanen says. The sharp rise in short-dated Treasury yields coupled with a decline in long-dated ones after Wednesday's September consumer-price inflation print suggest that risk sentiment is fragile, the chief rates strategist says. This, in turn, helps cap the upside in Treasury yields, the chief rates strategist says. "The coming days will be important in determining whether the move triggers a continued short-covering rally," he says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0530 GMT - Inflation remains the pivotal variable because it will influence both the direction of monetary policy and the path of government bond yields, Payden & Rygel's Laura Lake and Tim Crawmer say in a note. "If inflation cools more decisively, bonds could deliver price appreciation in addition to income," the senior strategists say. With inflation proving persistent and the possibility of further Fed rate increases, near-term returns may depend more heavily on carry, they add. Payden & Rygel, which prefers a "measured duration position rather than a heroic one," reckons that shorter-duration spread assets can generate incremental income and may help offset some weakness in government bonds if rates remain volatile. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0528 GMT - Payden & Rygel's exposure within U.S. fixed income has increasingly shifted toward the front end of the yield curve, senior strategists Laura Lake and Tim Crawmer say in a note. "Attractive starting yields, substantial tightening already reflected in prices, and greater sensitivity to any eventual change in Federal Reserve policy create a compelling combination," they say. More broadly, Payden & Rygel remains constructive on fixed income and credit spread risk, they say. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0521 GMT - Investors are being paid to own bonds again, Payden & Rygel's Laura Lake and Tim Crawmer say in a note. "All-in yields are attractive, corporate fundamentals remain broadly sound and demand for fixed income is robust," the senior strategists say. That gives investors a meaningful source of income while they wait for greater clarity on inflation and interest rates, they say. There is also the potential for more than income. If inflation moderates and government bond yields move lower, investors could benefit from capital appreciation as well, they add. "We do not expect the path to be smooth, but the starting yield provides a much better cushion than investors had during the long low-rate era." (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0513 GMT - Candriam remains underweight in French and Belgium government bonds, Nicolas Jullien, global head of fixed income says. "French spreads have widened substantially, but the lack of a clear path to fiscal adjustment and the approaching presidential election leave few catalysts for sustained improvement," he says in a note. France's average financing cost remains around 2%, but new borrowing costs exceed 4%, and with close to 40% of outstanding debt requiring refinancing over five years, persistently high yields would progressively increase the budget burden, he says. A credible fiscal program could support a rally. Uncertainty around France's fiscal prospects currently supports Bunds, but that relationship could reverse if the European Central Bank takes forceful action to contain sovereign spreads, he says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0513 GMT - Candriam maintains its duration overweight in the eurozone's rates universe, centered on the 10-year German Bund, alongside a 10-30-year steepening bias, says Nicolas Jullien, global head of fixed income, in a note. Candriam's valuation framework points to a Bund yield around 3.25%, allowing for another European Central Bank rate hike this year, he says. Markets price roughly three further hikes by summer 2027 after September's raise, a demanding path for an economy whose underlying growth prospects remain modest, he adds. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0350 GMT - The dollar will likely trade between 4.08 and 4.09 ringgit next week, Kenanga economists say in a note. Escalating U.S.-Iran tensions could keep oil prices and U.S. inflation expectations elevated, while September Malaysian inflation and trade data will be in focus, they say. They expect the Fed to raise rates by 25 bps in December and no moves in 2027, although markets are pricing in two further hikes. Stretched investor positioning could limit the dollar's gains, leaving the ringgit volatile but rangebound, they add. Kenanga expects the dollar to face resistance at 4.085 ringgit, with support at 4.081 ringgit. The dollar is flat at 4.0846 ringgit. (yingxian.wong@wsj.com)

0329 GMT - Evidence is mounting that 100 basis points of official-interest-rate increases this year by the Reserve Bank of Australia might be enough. Capital Economics economist Marcel Thieliant says the central bank's September rate increase has made policy more restrictive than even the central bank had thought. The tightening has taken its toll on activity and the job market, with the unemployment rate continuing to rise, he says. That should be enough to signal policy has been tightened sufficiently, though inflation will have to come off the boil before the hike cycle truly ends, he adds. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

0250 GMT - The Singapore dollar consolidates against its U.S. counterpart in the Asian session. The Singapore dollar may be aided by mostly lower U.S. Treasury yields that tend to diminish the appeal of U.S. fixed-income assets and demand for the greenback. From a technical analysis perspective, the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pair's "recent sharp spike higher may end as a false break," say strategists at OCBC Group Research in a report. "The spike has failed to build on momentum thus far," they add. The U.S. dollar is little changed at 1.2821 Singapore dollars, LSEG data show. (ronnie.harui@wsj.com)

0235 GMT - India's exports in September were strong, showing broad-based resilience across most products and destinations, Nomura analysts Aurodeep Nandi and Sonal Varma say in a note. Import growth also reflected steady demand across consumer, investment and industrial goods and commodities. However, the rising merchandise trade deficit masks the healthy export growth, the analysts say, and they expect the current account deficit to average 1.8% of GDP in FY 2027, up from 0.6% in FY26. (venkat.pr@wsj.com)

0220 GMT - The case for a rise in interest rates by the Reserve Bank of Australia in November has softened somewhat after news this week of weak employment data, says Adam Boyton, head of Australian economics at ANZ. Still Boyton expects an increase next month, but says coming 3Q inflation data are now more critical to the continuance of that call. The RBA's sensitivity to a softening job market has likely diminished, he adds. The September policy meeting minutes suggested the board has become more willing to accept some weakness in activity and employment in order to return inflation to target, he says. (james.glynn@wsj.com; Twitter @JamesGlynnWSJ)
